title: Real Talk About Latino Voters, with Felicia Escobar Carrillo
description: If you want to understand why Texas went blue, and what it takes to stay that way, you should listen to Felicia Escobar Carrillo. A native Texan herself, Felicia served in senior roles in the U.S. Senate, was a top immigration policy advisor in the Obama White House, and was chief of staff at U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services in the Biden administration. We’ll talk about how Texas Democrats up and down the ballot supported each other in a state the size of a country, why this was harder to pull off in Florida, and what “abolish ICE” means to Latino voters. Felicia’s verdict: Democrats are “on probation” with Latinos. Now the blue wave of governors and legislators needs to deliver relief on affordability and immigration policy, which are deeply connected.

title: The Diplomat, with Rena Bitter
description: Every day, all around the world, 13,000 U.S. Foreign Service Officers are responsible for a potentially life-changing decision: Should the person in front of me get a visa to the United States? Rena Bitter oversaw this global operation as Assistant Secretary of State for Consular Affairs, the capstone of her 30-year career as a diplomat and ambassador. Now retired, she can speak freely about how the visa process really works, and how Trump 2.0 is dramatically changing who gets to travel and study here, along with the nature of the Foreign Service itself. She also tells us what it took to carry out the largest airlift in American history to rescue our Afghan allies, why she loves international students, and how in government you have to know when the juice is worth the squeeze.

title: From Suing the Man to Serving the Man, with Lucas Guttentag
description: What happens when you spend decades suing the government, and then help run the government? Back in the 1980s, Lucas Guttentag started the Immigrant Rights Project at the ACLU. He and his team argued hugely consequential cases across the country and all the way to the Supreme Court, securing fundamental due process and nondiscrimination rights for the most vulnerable immigrant communities. Then, during the Obama and Biden eras, Lucas went to work for his longtime courtroom opponents: the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice. We’ll explore the games lawyers play, what it’s like to pursue change from inside a giant bureaucracy, how the courts became a potent weapon for anti-immigrant forces – and, in the end, how to win.

title: Asylum Is Not a Loophole, with Colleen Zengotitabengoa
description: What is asylum? Simply put, the United States must not return someone to a country where they have a well-founded fear of persecution. Following the atrocities of World War II, Congress created a U.S. asylum system under international treaty and federal law. But in recent years, as many more people sought asylum at the U.S./Mexico border, this moral and legal obligation became a political lightning rod. Colleen Zengotitabengoa has seen these challenges first-hand, in her two decades serving at the Department of Homeland Security, the White House, and Congress. As an attorney, she has directly represented asylum-seekers – real people who were not “exploiting a loophole.” Colleen will help you understand what happened to our asylum system, why it matters, and what we as a nation need to do next.

title: Confessions of an Immigration Bureaucrat, with Michael Valverde
description: Every year, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) makes millions of highly consequential decisions that affect individual people’s lives. Applications for green cards, work permits, asylum and refugee status, even U.S. citizenship – they’re all handled by the 20,000 civil servants at USCIS. The agency has always had its struggles, but under Trump 2.0, political appointees have actively undermined and targeted civil servants like never before. Michael Valverde dedicated his career to USCIS for three decades, working in roles throughout the agency and rising to senior management. Having taken early retirement after the DOGE debacle, he’s ready to pull back the curtain on how this agency really works: Why backlogs seem so endless, how immigration officers think, and what’s the difference between useful vs. useless security vetting. Michael also shares what he’s told countless new Americans at their citizenship ceremonies: Immigrants make our country richer.

title: Three Big Lies About Immigrants and Fraud, with Sonya Schwartz
description: From the first moments of his first campaign for president, Donald Trump has accused immigrants of fraudulently obtaining public benefits, immigration protections, and even votes. Does any of this hold up under scrutiny? We asked Sonya Schwartz, who knows more than just about anyone about the complex intersection of immigration, public benefits, and voting laws. She has the data to debunk all three of MAGA’s big lies about immigrants and fraud, and how this scapegoating leads to policies that harm all of us – from millions of families losing food assistance to voter ID laws that would block U.S. citizens from the polls. Meanwhile, some of the country’s worst actual fraudsters are getting pardoned instead of prosecuted.

description: In the 2024 presidential election, Republicans spent nearly $600 million on political advertisements pounding Biden (and then Harris) for botching the border. description: Jenny Hunt is a Rutgers University professor, the former Chief Economist at the Department of Labor, and a key contributor to the gold-standard, 600-page consensus report on the economic consequences of immigration. Economists agree that immigration makes native-born Americans wealthier on average, expands the U.S. economy, and has positive long-term effects on government budgets. The main debate is over the impact of immigration on the wages of Americans without a high school education – and they would be helped far more by a stronger social safety net than by restricting immigration. So what’s the anti-immigrant movement really about…?

summary:
Jenny Hunt is a Rutgers University professor, the former Chief Economist at the Department of Labor, and a key contributor to the gold-standard, 600-page consensus report on the economic consequences of immigration. Don’t worry, we’re going to summarize it together in 45 breezy minutes!

Economists agree that immigration makes native-born Americans wealthier on average, expands the U.S. economy, and has positive long-term effects on government budgets. The main debate is over the impact of immigration on the wages of Americans without a high school education – and they would be helped far more by a stronger social safety net than by restricting immigration. So what’s the anti-immigrant movement really about…?

title: The Truth About ICE, with Jason Houser
description: From calls to abolish ICE to deeply held misconceptions about immigration and criminality, few agencies generate more heat and less light than Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Jason Houser served as ICE Chief of Staff and joins us to sort out truth from fiction: Why is the Trump administration redirecting criminal law enforcement agents to civil deportation work? Is that akin to defunding the police? How many ICE officers actually need to be armed? And what should the future of this agency look like?
summary:
From calls to abolish ICE to deeply held misconceptions about immigration and criminality, few agencies generate more heat and less light than Immigration and Customs Enforcement. In this episode, we dig into the reality of how ICE actually operates, including the fact that the vast majority of people ICE arrests have no criminal record.

Jason Houser served as ICE Chief of Staff and is an Intelligence Officer in the Navy Reserve. He joins us to sort out truth from fiction: Why is the Trump administration redirecting criminal law enforcement agents to civil deportation work? Is that akin to defunding the police? How many ICE officers actually need to be armed? And what should the future of this agency look like?

Corrections: (1) Border Patrol has expanded checkpoint and search authorities within 100 miles of any land border or U.S. coastline. About two-thirds of the U.S. population live within this area, which includes Chicago, Los Angeles, and New York City (but not Minneapolis). See: Explainer: U.S. Border Patrol Authorities and the 100-Mile Border Zone – National Immigration Forum (March 31, 2026). (2) Alas, the Nicolas Cage character in National Treasure is “an American treasure hunter and cryptologist,” not an HSI agent. But the Harvey Keitel character is an FBI special agent in charge of hunting down antiquities! If the stolen Declaration of Independence crossed an international border, surely he’d pull in HSI…

title: DACA and the Dreamer Movement, with Felicia Escobar Carrillo
description: You may know about the plight of Dreamers – over 3 million undocumented individuals who were brought here as children and are Americans in every way but immigration status. And you may know about DACA, the Obama-era policy that has allowed 800,000 Dreamers to pursue higher education, military service, and life out of the shadows. But a quarter-century after the DREAM Act was first introduced, Congress still hasn’t provided permanent relief for Dreamers, and DACA is under threat. Felicia Escobar Carrillo was Special Assistant to the President for Immigration Policy in the Obama White House, and tells the story of how DACA was created – after intensive organizing by Dreamers who continue to carry the torch today.

title: The Birth of the Department of Homeland Security
description: After 9/11, the U.S. government undertook the largest federal reorganization since the creation of the Pentagon. The result was DHS — a sprawling mega-agency that absorbed immigration functions from three different departments. How did this reshuffling shape the immigration system we have today, and what did we lose in the process?
image_alt: Protesters with Never Again signs being detained by police at an immigration demonstration
transcript:
Claire Trickler-McNulty: Welcome back to The Melting Pod. Today we’re talking about something that fundamentally reshaped how America handles immigration — the creation of the Department of Homeland Security.

Doug Rand: Yeah, and I think most people don’t realize that before 2003, there was no DHS. Immigration was handled by the Immigration and Naturalization Service — the INS — which sat inside the Department of Justice.

Amanda Baran: And the INS was this fascinating, deeply dysfunctional agency that was responsible for both welcoming immigrants and deporting them. It was like having the same person be your defense attorney and the prosecutor.

Claire: Which is exactly why Congress decided to blow it up after 9/11. But the story of how DHS came together is really a story about the politics of fear, bureaucratic turf wars, and some genuinely consequential decisions made under enormous time pressure.

Doug: Let’s bring in our guest. Michael Chen served in senior roles at both the old INS and the new DHS during the transition. Michael, take us back to that moment…

[Transcript continues…]

title: The Rise and Fall of Comprehensive Immigration Reform
description: For decades, “comprehensive immigration reform” was the holy grail of immigration policy. From Reagan’s 1986 amnesty to the Gang of Eight, we trace how the grand bargain kept almost happening — and why it keeps falling apart.
image_alt: Two women wearing American flag headscarves sharing a moment of solidarity at a march

title: How Asylum and the Border Took Over American Politics
description: Asylum wasn’t always front-page news. We unpack how a legal protection created after World War II became the most politically explosive word in immigration — and what the current crackdown means for people fleeing danger.
